Prof. Divyansh: Binita, please sit. This paragraph reads very differently from your earlier work. Did you use an AI tool?
Binita: (heart pounding) ...Yes. Partly.
Prof. Divyansh: Which part?
Binita: The summary section, and I asked it to polish my sentences. The analysis is mine. I have my handwritten notes and the first draft here.
Prof. Divyansh: Thank you for saying so directly. Show me the notes.
Binita: (sliding over the pages) I didn't read the course rules properly. I thought polishing was fine.
Prof. Divyansh: The rule asks you to declare any use. Let's read it together, then we can decide what to do with this submission.
Binita: Okay. I should have asked first.

qa.q: Which parts did Binita say came from the AI tool?
qa.a: Binita said the summary section and the sentence polishing came from the tool, while the analysis was Binita's own.

qa.q: How did Binita feel when the professor asked about the AI tool, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Exposed and nervous: Binita's heart was pounding before the answer, which came after a pause.

qa.q: What did Binita do that kept a small matter small?
qa.a: Binita told the truth, showed handwritten notes and the first draft, and agreed to learn the rules, instead of lying.

qa.q: How might Prof. Divyansh see Binita's honesty?
qa.a: Prof. Divyansh thanked Binita for saying it directly, so honesty and visible process make it easier to treat this as a rule to learn than as cheating.

grounding: A professor suspects an AI-written assignment when it was partly so, and Binita admits it honestly, shows process and learns the rules.

"Sit, Disha." Professor Rekha turned the screen. "This essay reads very differently from your mid-term. The software flagged it. Did you write it?"

Disha's throat dried. "Mostly. The introduction... I asked the AI for one, and I changed some words."

"Only the introduction?"

"Yes, ma'am. The analysis is mine. I have my drafts." She opened her laptop with shaking hands. "These are my notes from the library, and three earlier versions."

The professor scrolled for a while in silence. "The body of the work does look like yours. Why didn't you just tell me at the start?"

"I didn't know if it was allowed. I thought everyone does it."

"The course policy is on page two of the outline. Read it. Rewrite the introduction yourself by Friday." A pause. "And thank you for not lying. That would have made this much worse."

qa.q: By when must Disha rewrite the introduction?
qa.a: Disha must rewrite the introduction by Friday.

qa.q: What was Disha feeling when the professor asked if she wrote the essay?
qa.a: Disha felt exposed and frightened; her dry throat and shaking hands show her fear of being caught.

qa.q: Which choice worked for Disha, and why?
qa.a: Admitting the AI-written introduction and showing her drafts worked, because honesty and proof of her process kept a small problem from becoming a serious one.

qa.q: How does Professor Rekha see Disha's honesty?
qa.a: Professor Rekha values it; being told the truth lets the professor treat it as a lesson about the rules rather than as cheating.

grounding: The dialogue shows a student suspected of AI-written work being honest, showing her process and learning the course rules.

passage:
It still makes my stomach turn a little, remembering that email from Professor Jagdish: "Please see me about your assignment. Possible AI generation." I'm Raghav, and half of that assignment was mine. The other half, the literature summary, came from a chatbot I had lightly edited.

My first plan was to deny everything. A classmate said that's what everyone does. But I remembered a senior who had lied in the same situation last year; when the logs came out, a small warning became a disciplinary hearing.

So I went in with my rough notebook and my search history, and I said it plainly: this part is mine, this part isn't. Professor Jagdish frowned, asked me to rewrite the summary, and cut some marks. It stung. But it ended there, and I read the college AI policy that night, properly.

qa.q: Which part of the assignment came from a chatbot?
qa.a: The literature summary came from a chatbot that Raghav had lightly edited.

qa.q: What was Raghav feeling when the professor's email arrived, and how can you tell?
qa.a: Raghav felt anxious and exposed; the memory still makes the stomach turn, and the first instinct was to deny everything.

qa.q: Why did telling the truth turn out better than denying it?
qa.a: Raghav remembered a senior's lie turning a warning into a disciplinary hearing, so honesty with notes kept the matter small.

qa.q: How might Professor Jagdish see Raghav's plain explanation?
qa.a: Professor Jagdish may still be disappointed, but can see a student willing to show the process and take responsibility, which makes fair action possible.

grounding: The reflection shows a student suspected of AI-written work choosing honesty, showing the process and learning the rules instead of lying.
